evidence.claim: Water helped decide which town would keep the railroad.

evidence.claim: When Union Pacific reached Green River in 1868, its officials found an established town and moved their planned division point 12 miles west to Bryan on Blacks Fork.
evidence.quote: They moved the division point 12 miles (19 km) west, creating the town of Bryan, on the Blacks Fork of the Green River.

evidence.claim: When Union Pacific reached Green River in 1868, its officials found an established town
evidence.quote: The Union Pacific Railroad reached Green River on October 1, 1868, and was supposed to be the site of a division point for the railroad. Railroad officials were surprised to find that a town of 2000 residents and permanent adobe buildings had been established there

evidence.claim: Then drought dried up Blacks Fork, forcing the railroad back to Green River for locomotive water; Bryan became a ghost town.
evidence.quote: Blacks Fork dried up during a drought and the railroad was forced to move the division point back to Green River to ensure adequate water for its steam locomotives. Bryan became the ghost town.

evidence.claim: The surviving original downtown core now forms a historic district that includes the Union Pacific depot.

The district includes 11 contributing buildings and one other contributing structure, including the Union Pacific Depot.

evidence.claim: Flaming Gorge Reservoir covers a narrow, steep-sided canyon whose rock includes sandstone and hard quartzite interspersed with softer layers.
evidence.quote: The foundation of the reservoir is a narrow, steep-sided canyon composed of siliceous sandstone and hard quartzites inter-bedded with softer shales, siltstones, and argillites.

evidence.claim: Construction of the dam began in 1958 and ended in 1964, impounding the Green River.
evidence.quote: Flaming Gorge Reservoir is the largest reservoir in  Wyoming, on the Green River, impounded behind the Flaming Gorge Dam. Construction on the dam began in 1958 and was completed in 1964.

evidence.claim: Most of the reservoir lies in southwestern Wyoming, with part in northeastern Utah.
evidence.quote: The reservoir is mainly in southwest Wyoming and partially in northeastern Utah.

evidence.claim: Dutch John, Utah, was built as a construction base and then an administrative site.
evidence.quote: The nearby town of Dutch John, Utah, was built to serve as a base camp during construction of the dam, and as an administrative site afterwards.
